lines.text: It's eighteen forty six, and a woman in labour arrives at Vienna General Hospital.
If she gets a fever after the birth and dies, any doctor here will tell you why. Bad air.
The hospital has two maternity clinics. In the first, one mother in nine dies. Yet in the second, it's one in thirty six.
But here's what nobody can explain: why does it matter so much which day she walks in?
They take women in on alternate days.
Doctors and medical students run the first one, and midwives run the second.
And the women know it, so well that they beg on their knees to be taken anywhere else.
Please. Not the first clinic.
Same building. Same city. Same air. So if you were the doctor here, what would you check first?
That question eats at a young doctor called Ignaz Semmelweis. He's twenty eight, and the new assistant in the first clinic.
Everything was in question. Only the large number of deaths was an unquestionable reality.
So Semmelweis starts testing his guesses, one at a time.
Maybe it's the air. Yet women who give birth in the street, on their way to the hospital, hardly ever catch the fever.
Maybe it's how they give birth. The midwives' mothers lie on their side, so he has the women in his clinic do the same.
Nothing changes.
Maybe it's fear. Whenever a woman is dying, a priest comes through the ward to her bed, and a man walks ahead of him ringing a bell.
Even to me myself it had a strange effect upon my nerves, when I heard the bell hurry past my door.
So he sends the priest the long way round, but the mothers keep dying.
By now, whatever you guessed first, he's probably tried it. And every time, he was wrong.
Then, in March eighteen forty seven, his friend Jakob Kolletschka, a professor of forensic medicine, is cut by a student's knife during an autopsy. And he dies.
Day and night I was haunted by the image of Kolletschka's disease.
And when they examine his friend's body, they find something he can't shake. It's the same disease that's killing the mothers.
Now think about who does the autopsies in this hospital.
The doctors. The students. The same people who walk from the morgue straight to the mothers in the first clinic.
With the same bare hands.
So what are those hands carrying?
Semmelweis is about to find out.
And what happens next will change medicine.
But first, he'll have to convince a world that doesn't want to listen.
